To a large extent species and subspecies on the Secretary's present list of animals threatened with worldwide extinction are those which have been decimated by overexploitation for the purposes of trade. Some of the less conspicuous forms which have no trade value may be seriously threatened by natural or man-made environmental factors, but the plight of the population may go unnoticed because knowledge of the current status of the population is lacking. Although North American populations are probably more thoroughly studied than those in other parts of the world, data on population status of many species are lacking here as well.
In the United States the physical environment that will be affected by successful implementation of the proposed legislation will be determined in two ways: (1) Most endangered species and subspecies are geographical isolates whose restoration will affect a rather small segment of the environment even if it is possible to restore the animal to all of its former range.

(2) A somewhat smaller number of species and subspecies are wide-ranging, and in a portion of that range may be characteristic of one biome. Only a few species, however, can be considered dominant members of any biome.

Collectively, of course, an important segment of the American environment will be affected, but at no time are the species and subspecies listed as endangered expected to represent all geographical areas of the United States or all biomes equally.
